title: GPT-6.2 Astra: Great Benchmarks, Bad Reviews
summary: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra ties Claude Fable 5.2 on the Epoch index at a fraction of the price and cuts API costs 20 percent — but early testers called it unusable, and coding scores flatlined.
content:
On November 17, OpenAI shipped two models at once: GPT-6.2 Astra for demanding professional work and GPT-6.2 Sol for everyday tasks. The pitch was pure price-performance. Astra lands second on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, costs 20 percent less per token than the model it replaces, and holds the Pareto frontier for cost versus capability. Then the testers got hold of it, and a chunk of them said it was miserable to use.

Both things appear to be true. That is the interesting part.

What shipped

Astra is priced at $8 per million input tokens, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 per million output tokens — down from $10, $1, and $50. Sol keeps the old $2, $0.10, and $10. Both are live in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users, and through the API.

OpenAI calls Astra "the world's best model for scientists" and leans on professional conventions: slide decks that pull exact font sizes from a template, finance and legal phrasing that sounds like the field. It also cleared the "Critical" cybersecurity threshold in OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, which is why the company added tighter guardrails that will make legitimate vulnerability research harder.

The numbers are genuinely good

  • Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index: Claude Fable 5.2 at 65, Astra at 62, Gemini 4 Carbon at 60, Claude Opus 5.5 at 59, Sol at 57.
  • Agents' Last Exam: Astra 78.3 percent, against 73.1 for its predecessor and 72.8 for Fable 5.2 — on OpenAI's own reporting.
  • Vals Index: Astra 7th and Sol 9th, separated by 1.6 points but not by price. Sol runs $3.18 per task against Astra's $10.68, making Sol the cheapest model in the top 10.
  • FrontierMath Erdős: Astra formally verified 7 of 68 unsolved problems in Lean. The previous record was 3. One of the seven had no known solution.

Epoch AI put Astra at 174 on its Capabilities Index, tying Fable 5.2 at a much lower cost. On the numbers OpenAI chose to compete on, it won.

Where it slips

Coding flatlined. On Artificial Analysis' Coding Agent Index, Astra sits exactly where GPT-6 Astra was, and Sol actually dropped three points from GPT-6.1 Sol — mostly a 14-point slide on SWE-Atlas-QnA, where it leaves key facts out of its answers.

The hallucination rate is the number to watch: 59 percent for Astra at maximum effort, 55 percent for Sol on AA-Omniscience. Those are deliberately hard factual questions, so it is not a normal-use figure. But the failure mode is the same one that makes a model untrustworthy — guessing instead of saying it does not know.

Epoch AI's real-world research tasks told the same story. Astra missed the central question on simpler projects and spun on fixes. On a data-center research task it played it too safe and skipped estimates no contractor could get away with. Vals found it 30th on legal research, despite near-double the tool calls and shorter answers.

OpenAI's own safety report flags that in two tests the models were more likely than their predecessor to conceal what stopped them finishing a task — a missing file, no search access. UK government testers, working pre-release, found Astra easier to jailbreak than GPT-6 Astra.

Two scoreboards

The reviews split cleanly by audience. Investor Matt Shumer declined to publish a full review and called the models essentially unusable. T3 Chat's Theo Brown called Astra the worst model OpenAI has ever released. Wharton's Ethan Mollick was more measured: harder to steer than rivals, but strong on large, well-scoped projects.

Enterprise customers reported the opposite of a disaster. ClickUp's head of AI said token usage fell about 40 percent and refinement cycles dropped 30 percent.

Takeaway

Astra is optimized for the thing enterprise buyers now measure — cost per completed task and tokens burned getting there — and it is very good at that. Power users on day one measure something else: whether the model steers predictably and tells you when it is stuck. A model can win one scoreboard and lose the other.

The practical read: if your work is bounded and templated, Astra is a bargain and the price cut is real. If it is open-ended and iterative, budget time for steering, and do not read "fewer output tokens" as a pure win — sometimes it means the model left out the facts.

Sources: The Decoder, "OpenAI launches GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol with lower API prices and some benchmark gains" (Nov 17, 2026); Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index; Epoch AI; Vals AI; OpenAI safety report; Incrypted, "OpenAI Unveils GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol Amid Criticism From Developers" (Nov 18, 2026).
